claim: Piezo1 is highly expressed in mouse skin.
source: Analysis of Piezo channel mRNA expression in mouse tissues has previously shown that Piezo1 is highly expressed in skin, while Piezo2 is less abundant (Coste et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Coste et al., 2010.

claim: Piezo2 is less abundant in mouse skin compared to Piezo1.
source: Analysis of Piezo channel mRNA expression in mouse tissues has previously shown that Piezo1 is highly expressed in skin, while Piezo2 is less abundant (Coste et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Coste et al., 2010.

claim: PIEZO1 is highly expressed in the epidermal layer of keratinocytes.
source: LacZ staining of skin tissue from these reporter mice revealed a high expression of PIEZO1 in the epidermal layer of keratinocytes as well as in hair follicles (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by LacZ staining data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: PIEZO1 is highly expressed in hair follicles.
source: LacZ staining of skin tissue from these reporter mice revealed a high expression of PIEZO1 in the epidermal layer of keratinocytes as well as in hair follicles (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by LacZ staining data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Global knockout of Piezo1 is embryonically lethal.
source: Since the global knockout of Piezo1 is embryonically lethal (Li et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014), we generated an epidermal-specific knockout mouse to investigate whether PIEZO1 plays a role in cutaneous wound healing.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2014 and Ranade et al., 2014.

claim: Krt14Cre;Piezo1fl/fl mice are viable.
source: The Krt14Cre mouse line was crossed with Piezo1fl/fl mice (Cahalan et al., 2015) to generate Krt14Cre;Piezo1fl/fl mice (hereafter referred to as conditional knockout, cKO) which are viable, develop normally, and feature normal skin sections (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with observations by Moehring et al., 2020.
evidence: The claim is supported by observations in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation to Moehring et al., 2020.

claim: Krt14Cre;Piezo1fl/fl mice develop normally.
source: The Krt14Cre mouse line was crossed with Piezo1fl/fl mice (Cahalan et al., 2015) to generate Krt14Cre;Piezo1fl/fl mice (hereafter referred to as conditional knockout, cKO) which are viable, develop normally, and feature normal skin sections (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with observations by Moehring et al., 2020.
evidence: The claim is supported by observations in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation to Moehring et al., 2020.

claim: Krt14Cre;Piezo1fl/fl mice feature normal skin sections.
source: The Krt14Cre mouse line was crossed with Piezo1fl/fl mice (Cahalan et al., 2015) to generate Krt14Cre;Piezo1fl/fl mice (hereafter referred to as conditional knockout, cKO) which are viable, develop normally, and feature normal skin sections (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with observations by Moehring et al., 2020.
evidence: The claim is supported by observations in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation to Moehring et al., 2020.

claim: Piezo1 mRNA expression is efficiently abrogated in keratinocytes from Piezo1-cKO animals.
source: qRT-PCR analysis using keratinocytes harvested from Piezo1-cKO and littermate control animals confirmed expression of Piezo1 and not Piezo2 in control mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and showed that Piezo1 mRNA expression is efficiently abrogated in cells from cKO animals (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Control keratinocytes express Piezo1 and not Piezo2.
source: qRT-PCR analysis using keratinocytes harvested from Piezo1-cKO and littermate control animals confirmed expression of Piezo1 and not Piezo2 in control mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and showed that Piezo1 mRNA expression is efficiently abrogated in cells from cKO animals (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Piezo1 produces Ca2+ flickers in adherent cells in response to cell-generated forces in the absence of external mechanical stimulation.
source: We previously reported that in adherent cells Piezo1 produces Ca2+ flickers in response to cell-generated forces in the absence of external mechanical stimulation (Pathak et al., 2014; Ellefsen et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pathak et al., 2014 and Ellefsen et al., 2019.

claim: Keratinocytes from Piezo1-cKO mice showed a 63% reduction in Ca2+ flickers compared to littermate control cells.
source: Compared to littermate control (ControlcKO) cells, keratinocytes from Piezo1-cKO mice showed a 63% reduction in Ca2+ flickers, indicating that a majority of Ca2+ flickers arise from cell-generated activation of the PIEZO1 channel (Figure 1C, D, E, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 1C, D, E.

claim: A majority of Ca2+ flickers arise from cell-generated activation of the PIEZO1 channel.
source: Compared to littermate control (ControlcKO) cells, keratinocytes from Piezo1-cKO mice showed a 63% reduction in Ca2+ flickers, indicating that a majority of Ca2+ flickers arise from cell-generated activation of the PIEZO1 channel (Figure 1C, D, E, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the 63% reduction in Ca2+ flickers in Piezo1-cKO cells.

claim: Piezo1-GoF cells displayed a nearly threefold increase in the frequency of Ca2+ flickers relative to littermate controls.
source: Piezo1-GoF cells displayed a nearly threefold increase in the frequency of Ca2+ flickers relative to littermate controls (ControlGoF) (Figure 1F, G, H. Figure 1—video 2), further supporting PIEZO1 as a key source of Ca2+ flickers.
evidence: The claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 1F, G, H.

claim: Six days post wounding, Piezo1-cKO mice displayed significantly smaller wound areas relative to their control littermates.
source: Six days post wounding, Piezo1-cKO mice displayed significantly smaller wound areas relative to their control littermates, while Piezo1-GoF mice showed larger wound areas, suggesting that increased channel activity leads to impaired rates of wound closure (Figure 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo wound healing data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Piezo1-GoF mice showed larger wound areas six days post wounding compared to control littermates.
source: Six days post wounding, Piezo1-cKO mice displayed significantly smaller wound areas relative to their control littermates, while Piezo1-GoF mice showed larger wound areas, suggesting that increased channel activity leads to impaired rates of wound closure (Figure 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo wound healing data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Increased PIEZO1 channel activity leads to impaired rates of wound closure.
source: Six days post wounding, Piezo1-cKO mice displayed significantly smaller wound areas relative to their control littermates, while Piezo1-GoF mice showed larger wound areas, suggesting that increased channel activity leads to impaired rates of wound closure (Figure 1J).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Piezo1-GoF mice showed larger wound areas.

claim: Scratches in monolayers of Piezo1-cKO keratinocytes closed faster than those from littermate ControlcKO cells.
source: Scratches in monolayers of Piezo1-cKO keratinocytes closed faster than those from littermate ControlcKO cells (Figure 1L, left).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro scratch assay data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Scratch closure in monolayers of Piezo1-GoF keratinocytes was significantly slower than control.
source: Conversely, scratch closure in monolayers of Piezo1-GoF keratinocytes was significantly slower (Figure 1L, middle).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro scratch assay data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: When the PIEZO1 agonist Yoda1 was added to healing ControlcKO monolayers at concentrations greater than 2 μM, scratch wound closure was significantly impaired.
source: Correspondingly, when the PIEZO1 agonist Yoda1 was added to healing ControlcKO monolayers at concentrations greater than 2 μM, scratch wound closure was also significantly impaired (Figure 1L, right, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), further supporting PIEZO1 involvement in re-epithelialization.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro scratch assay data shown in Figure 1L and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: No effect on wound closure was observed when Piezo1-cKO monolayers were treated with Yoda1.
source: No effect on wound closure was observed when Piezo1-cKO monolayers were treated with Yoda1 indicating that inhibition of scratch closure is the result of PIEZO1 activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro scratch assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Inhibition of scratch closure by Yoda1 is the result of PIEZO1 activity.
source: No effect on wound closure was observed when Piezo1-cKO monolayers were treated with Yoda1 indicating that inhibition of scratch closure is the result of PIEZO1 activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Yoda1 has no effect on Piezo1-cKO monolayers.

claim: The PIEZO1 ion channel plays an important role in wound healing.
source: Collectively, our in vitro and in vivo data demonstrate that the PIEZO1 ion channel plays an important role in wound healing, with Piezo1 knockout accelerating the healing process (Figure 1M).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple in vitro and in vivo experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Piezo1 knockout accelerates the wound healing process.
source: Collectively, our in vitro and in vivo data demonstrate that the PIEZO1 ion channel plays an important role in wound healing, with Piezo1 knockout accelerating the healing process (Figure 1M).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple in vitro and in vivo experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Piezo1-cKO keratinocytes explored a larger area compared to littermate ControlcKO cells.
source: Interestingly, Piezo1-cKO keratinocytes explored a larger area compared to littermate ControlcKO cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by mean squared displacement analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The direction autocorrelation function for trajectories from Piezo1-cKO keratinocytes decayed slower than for littermate ControlcKO cells.
source: The direction autocorrelation function for trajectories from Piezo1-cKO keratinocytes decayed slower than for littermate ControlcKO cells, indicative of fewer turns and a straighter trajectory (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by direction autocorrelation analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Slower decay of direction autocorrelation is indicative of fewer turns and a straighter trajectory.
source: The direction autocorrelation function for trajectories from Piezo1-cKO keratinocytes decayed slower than for littermate ControlcKO cells, indicative of fewer turns and a straighter trajectory (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about direction autocorrelation analysis.

claim: The average instantaneous speed was higher for Piezo1-cKO cells relative to littermate ControlcKO cells.
source: The average instantaneous speed calculated by DiPer analysis was higher for Piezo1-cKO cells relative to littermate ControlcKO cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by speed analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Piezo1-cKO keratinocytes migrate significantly faster and straighter.
source: Thus, Piezo1-cKO keratinocytes migrate significantly faster and straighter.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the MSD, direction autocorrelation, and speed analyses.

claim: Piezo1-GoF keratinocytes explored a somewhat larger area compared to littermate ConGoF cells.
source: We observed that Piezo1-GoF keratinocytes also explored a somewhat larger area compared to littermate ConGoF cells, due to the cells migrating straighter with no difference in cell speed (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by MSD analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Piezo1-GoF keratinocytes migrate straighter with no difference in cell speed compared to control.
source: We observed that Piezo1-GoF keratinocytes also explored a somewhat larger area compared to littermate ConGoF cells, due to the cells migrating straighter with no difference in cell speed (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by direction autocorrelation and speed analyses shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: PIEZO1 regulates keratinocyte migration.
source: Overall, our data demonstrate that PIEZO1 regulates keratinocyte migration, with channel knockout resulting in faster migration speed.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple migration assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: PIEZO1 channel knockout results in faster migration speed.
source: Overall, our data demonstrate that PIEZO1 regulates keratinocyte migration, with channel knockout resulting in faster migration speed.
evidence: The claim is supported by speed analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Both Piezo1 knockout and the GoF mutation resulted in straighter trajectories.
source: The effects of the GoF mutation were more complex, and both Piezo1 knockout and the GoF mutation resulted in straighter trajectories.
evidence: The claim is supported by direction autocorrelation analyses shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3D.

claim: PIEZO1-tdTomato shows higher levels at the rear end of single migrating keratinocytes.
source: Here, we directly imaged endogenous PIEZO1-tdTomato's subcellular localization in individual live, migrating keratinocytes using TIRF imaging and noticed higher PIEZO1 levels at the rear end of the cell (Figure 3A, Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by TIRF imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: PIEZO1-tdTomato enrichment at the rear of single migrating cells suggests that PIEZO1 may underlie cell polarization during migration.
source: This observation of PIEZO1-tdTomato enrichment at the rear of single migrating cells suggests that PIEZO1 may underlie cell polarization during migration.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observation of PIEZO1 localization.

claim: Piezo1-cKO reduced the proportion of highly polarized shapes and increased the proportion of weakly polarized shapes relative to littermate ControlcKO keratinocytes.
source: VAMPIRE classification of the Piezo1-cKO and littermate ControlcKO keratinocytes into 20 shape modes revealed that Piezo1-cKO reduced the proportion of highly polarized shapes and increased the proportion of weakly polarized shapes relative to littermate ControlcKO keratinocytes (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by VAMPIRE shape mode analysis shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: The GoF mutation increased the frequency of polarized and hyper-polarized shapes at the expense of unpolarized or weakly polarized cell shapes.
source: On the other hand, the GoF mutation increased the frequency of polarized and hyper-polarized shapes at the expense of unpolarized or weakly polarized cell shapes (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by VAMPIRE shape mode analysis shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: PIEZO1 activity promotes cell polarization.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that PIEZO1 activity promotes cell polarization.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the VAMPIRE shape mode analyses.

claim: PIEZO1 activity promotes cell polarization through regulation of the channel's subcellular localization.
source: Based on imaging the localization of endogenous PIEZO1 channels in migrating cells, it appears that this may be mediated by regulation of the channel's subcellular localization.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on imaging data of PIEZO1 localization.

claim: At some regions along the wound margin, PIEZO1-tdTomato was enriched in band-like structures.
source: We found that at some regions along the wound margin, PIEZO1-tdTomato was enriched in band-like structures (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by TIRF imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: PIEZO1-tdTomato enrichment was observed a few hours after scratch generation.
source: Interestingly, this enrichment, which was observed a few hours after scratch generation (compare Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4A), was also highly dynamic, such that it ebbed and flowed over the course of imaging (Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of images in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4A.

claim: PIEZO1-tdTomato enrichment was highly dynamic, ebbing and flowing over the course of imaging.
source: Interestingly, this enrichment, which was observed a few hours after scratch generation (compare Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4A), was also highly dynamic, such that it ebbed and flowed over the course of imaging (Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 4—video 1.

claim: In fields of view that exhibited PIEZO1-tdTomato puncta enrichment at the wound edge, this channel enrichment was followed by a localized retraction of the wound edge.
source: In fields of view that exhibited PIEZO1-tdTomato puncta enrichment at the wound edge, this channel enrichment was followed by a localized retraction of the wound edge (Figure 4C, Figure 4E, Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by kymograph analysis shown in Figure 4C and 4E.

claim: 72% of PIEZO1-tdTomato enrichment tracks displayed a negative slope corresponding to cell edge retraction.
source: Kymobutler analysis of PIEZO1-tdTomato tracks overlaid on the DIC kymographs allowed examination of the migration dynamics of the wound edge in relation to Piezo1 enrichment (Figure 4E); 72% of these PIEZO1-tdTomato enrichment tracks displayed a negative slope corresponding to cell edge retraction and aligned with retraction events (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kymobutler analysis shown in Figure 4E and 4G.

claim: Enrichment of PIEZO1-tdTomato puncta resulted in wound edge retraction.
source: Thus, enrichment of PIEZO1-tdTomato puncta resulted in wound edge retraction (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the kymograph analyses showing correlation between PIEZO1 enrichment and retraction.

claim: The rear end of single migrating cells is the site of cellular retraction.
source: Importantly, the rear end of single migrating cells, where PIEZO1 is found to localize (Figure 3A), is also the site of cellular retraction (Petrie et al., 2009; Yam, 2007), suggesting a general relationship between PIEZO1 localization and retraction.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Petrie et al., 2009 and Yam, 2007.

claim: There is a general relationship between PIEZO1 localization and retraction.
source: Importantly, the rear end of single migrating cells, where PIEZO1 is found to localize (Figure 3A), is also the site of cellular retraction (Petrie et al., 2009; Yam, 2007), suggesting a general relationship between PIEZO1 localization and retraction.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PIEZO1 localizes to the rear where retraction occurs.

claim: Under control conditions, the cell edge displayed cycles of protrusion and retraction.
source: We observed that under control conditions, the cell edge displayed cycles of protrusion and retraction which was expected since cell migration is known to progress by iterative cycles of protrusion and retraction (Giannone et al., 2004; Giannone et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by kymograph analysis and citations to Giannone et al., 2004 and 2007.

claim: Cell migration progresses by iterative cycles of protrusion and retraction.
source: We observed that under control conditions, the cell edge displayed cycles of protrusion and retraction which was expected since cell migration is known to progress by iterative cycles of protrusion and retraction (Giannone et al., 2004; Giannone et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Giannone et al., 2004 and 2007.

claim: PIEZO1 activation by 4 μM Yoda1 greatly affected cell edge cycles and resulted in an extremely dynamic cell edge.
source: PIEZO1 activation by 4 μM Yoda1 greatly affected these cycles and resulted in an extremely dynamic cell edge (Figure 5A, Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by kymograph analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The frequency as well as the speed of cell edge retractions and protrusions increased upon Yoda1 treatment.
source: The frequency as well as the speed of cell edge retractions and protrusions increased upon Yoda1 treatment but resulted in a net cellular retraction over time (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), with some cells demonstrating drastic retraction with Yoda1 treatment (Figure 5—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by kymograph analysis shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Yoda1 treatment resulted in a net cellular retraction over time.
source: The frequency as well as the speed of cell edge retractions and protrusions increased upon Yoda1 treatment but resulted in a net cellular retraction over time (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), with some cells demonstrating drastic retraction with Yoda1 treatment (Figure 5—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by kymograph analysis shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Piezo1-cKO keratinocytes did not show an increase in retraction upon treatment with 4 μM Yoda1.
source: Piezo1-cKO keratinocytes did not show an increase in retraction upon treatment with 4 μM Yoda1 (Figure 5B and , Figure 5—video 3, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that Yoda1-induced increase in retraction is mediated by PIEZO1.
evidence: The claim is supported by kymograph analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Yoda1-induced increase in retraction is mediated by PIEZO1.
source: Piezo1-cKO keratinocytes did not show an increase in retraction upon treatment with 4 μM Yoda1 (Figure 5B and , Figure 5—video 3, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that Yoda1-induced increase in retraction is mediated by PIEZO1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Yoda1 has no effect on Piezo1-cKO cells.

claim: Kymographs of Piezo1-GoF keratinocytes showed an increase in cell edge dynamics compared to littermate ControlGoF cells.
source: Additionally, kymographs of Piezo1-GoF keratinocytes also showed an increase in cell edge dynamics compared to littermate ControlGoF cells further supporting PIEZO1's role in retraction (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—video 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by kymograph analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Yoda1 treatment resulted in a significant increase in edge velocities compared to DMSO-treated ControlcKO cells.
source: Yoda1 treatment resulted in a significant increase in edge velocities compared to DMSO-treated ControlcKO cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ADAPT analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Yoda1 resulted in an increase of cell edge velocity during both protrusion and retraction events, though the increase in retraction velocity was greater.
source: Yoda1, which is expected to globally activate PIEZO1 channels, resulted in an increase of cell edge velocity during both protrusion and retraction events, though the increase in retraction velocity was greater.
evidence: The claim is supported by ADAPT analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Piezo1-cKO keratinocytes showed a reduction in edge velocities relative to littermate ControlcKO cells.
source: In contrast, Piezo1-cKO keratinocytes showed a reduction in edge velocities relative to littermate ControlcKO cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by ADAPT analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Piezo1-GoF keratinocytes showed a significant increase in edge velocities relative to littermate ControlGoF.
source: Consistent with our observations of Yoda1 treatment, Piezo1-GoF keratinocytes also showed a significant increase in edge velocities relative to littermate ControlGoF (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by ADAPT analysis shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was a clear increase in the proportion of retracting positions relative to protruding positions in GoF keratinocytes.
source: Interestingly, there was a clear increase in the proportion of retracting positions relative to protruding positions in GoF keratinocytes.
evidence: The claim is supported by ADAPT analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: PIEZO1 activity regulates cell edge dynamics.
source: These results reveal that PIEZO1 activity regulates cell edge dynamics and further support our observations that PIEZO1 activity increases cellular retraction.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the ADAPT analyses of cell edge velocities.

claim: PIEZO1 activity increases cellular retraction.
source: These results reveal that PIEZO1 activity regulates cell edge dynamics and further support our observations that PIEZO1 activity increases cellular retraction.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple kymograph and ADAPT analyses.

claim: Monolayers of control keratinocytes advanced forward into the cell-free space under DMSO-treated control conditions.
source: Monolayers of control keratinocytes advanced forward into the cell-free space under DMSO-treated control conditions (Figure 5F, Figure 5—video 5), while the presence of 4 μM Yoda1 increased retraction events which prevented the monolayer from advancing far into the wound bed (Figure 5G, Figure 5—video 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by kymograph analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The presence of 4 μM Yoda1 increased retraction events which prevented the monolayer from advancing far into the wound bed.
source: Monolayers of control keratinocytes advanced forward into the cell-free space under DMSO-treated control conditions (Figure 5F, Figure 5—video 5), while the presence of 4 μM Yoda1 increased retraction events which prevented the monolayer from advancing far into the wound bed (Figure 5G, Figure 5—video 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by kymograph analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: In 35% of fields of view monitored in scratch assays, Yoda1 treatment resulted in an increase in scratch area instead of wound closure.
source: Remarkably, in 35% of fields of view monitored in scratch assays we observed that Yoda1 treatment resulted in an increase in scratch area instead of wound closure (Figure 1L).
evidence: The claim is supported by scratch assay data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: In Piezo1-cKO monolayers, cells protrude forward into the cell-free space to close scratch wounds to a greater extent than controls.
source: In Piezo1-cKO monolayers we observed cells protrude forward into the cell-free space to close scratch wounds to a greater extent than controls (Figure 5H, Figure 5—video 6), while GoF monolayers did so to a lower extent (Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Figure 5—video 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by kymograph analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: GoF monolayers protrude forward into the cell-free space to a lower extent than controls.
source: In Piezo1-cKO monolayers we observed cells protrude forward into the cell-free space to close scratch wounds to a greater extent than controls (Figure 5H, Figure 5—video 6), while GoF monolayers did so to a lower extent (Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Figure 5—video 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by kymograph analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: No effect of Yoda1 addition was seen on the rate of advancement in kymographs taken at the wound edge of Piezo1-cKO monolayers.
source: Additionally, no effect of Yoda1 addition was seen on the rate of advancement in kymographs taken at the wound edge of Piezo1-cKO monolayers (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by kymograph analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: PIEZO1 activity increases cellular retraction in keratinocytes, both in single cells and monolayers.
source: Collectively, our results show that PIEZO1 activity increases cellular retraction in keratinocytes, both in single cells and monolayers, which has a net effect on cell migration.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple kymograph and ADAPT analyses in Figure 5.

claim: PIEZO1 induces cellular retraction to slow single and collective cell migration and thus causes delayed wound healing.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate that PIEZO1 induces cellular retraction to slow single and collective cell migration and thus causes delayed wound healing.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of migration and wound healing assays.

claim: Dynamic enrichment of the channel protein serves to locally amplify channel activity and the downstream retraction events.
source: We propose that dynamic enrichment of the channel protein serves to locally amplify channel activity and the downstream retraction events.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on observations of PIEZO1 localization dynamics.

claim: In wound healing monolayers of keratinocytes, PIEZO1 enrichment and the subsequent wound edge retraction provide a molecular mechanism for how PIEZO1 slows wound healing.
source: In wound healing monolayers of keratinocytes, PIEZO1 enrichment and the subsequent wound edge retraction provide a molecular mechanism for how PIEZO1 slows wound healing, while absence of the channel accelerates wound healing.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of PIEZO1 localization and wound healing assays.

claim: Absence of PIEZO1 accelerates wound healing.
source: In wound healing monolayers of keratinocytes, PIEZO1 enrichment and the subsequent wound edge retraction provide a molecular mechanism for how PIEZO1 slows wound healing, while absence of the channel accelerates wound healing.
evidence: The claim is supported by wound healing assays in Piezo1-cKO mice.

claim: Epidermal-specific Piezo1 knockout resulted in faster wound healing in mice.
source: Our findings demonstrate that epidermal-specific Piezo1 knockout resulted in faster wound healing in mice, and conversely a Piezo1-GoF mutation slowed wound healing.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo wound healing data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: A Piezo1-GoF mutation slowed wound healing.
source: Our findings demonstrate that epidermal-specific Piezo1 knockout resulted in faster wound healing in mice, and conversely a Piezo1-GoF mutation slowed wound healing.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo wound healing data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: PIEZO1 activity modulated by dynamic spatial reorganization of the channel protein slows keratinocyte cell migration during re-epithelialization.
source: We recapitulate this observation in vitro, and show through a combination of orthogonal assays in single cells and in monolayers that PIEZO1 activity modulated by dynamic spatial reorganization of the channel protein slows keratinocyte cell migration during re-epithelialization.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of in vitro migration and localization assays.

claim: Targeted inhibition of PIEZO1 could help speed wound healing, potentially reducing risk of infection.
source: These findings provide physiological evidence for the role of a mechanically activated ion channel in wound healing and suggest potential therapeutics through a targeted inhibition of PIEZO1, perhaps applied topically, that could help speed wound healing, potentially reducing risk of infection.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the findings that PIEZO1 inhibition accelerates wound healing.

claim: Further in-depth analysis regarding the quality of wound healing following PIEZO1 inhibition is required.
source: However, further in-depth analysis regarding the quality of wound healing following PIEZO1 inhibition is required.
evidence: The claim acknowledges the need for additional research.

claim: Keratinocyte PIEZO1 is critical for sensory afferent firing and behavioral responses to innocuous and noxious mechanical stimulation.
source: Consistent with the latter idea, a recent study by Moehring et al. reports that keratinocyte PIEZO1 is critical for sensory afferent firing and behavioral responses to innocuous and noxious mechanical stimulation (Moehring et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Moehring et al., 2020.

claim: It would be important to determine that inhibiting Piezo1 to speed wound healing does not have detrimental effects on normal mechanosensation.
source: As such, it would also be important to determine that inhibiting Piezo1 to speed wound healing does not have detrimental effects on normal mechanosensation.
evidence: The claim is speculative, suggesting a need for future research.

claim: Ca2+ signals control many aspects of cell migration, including lamellipodial dynamics, traction force generation, rear retraction, focal adhesion turnover, and migration directionality.
source: Ca2+ signals control many aspects of cell migration, including lamellipodial dynamics, traction force generation, rear retraction, focal adhesion turnover, and migration directionality (Wei et al., 2012; Tsai et al., 2015; Canales et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wei et al., 2012, Tsai et al., 2015, and Canales et al., 2019.

claim: Mechanically activated ion channels were proposed to contribute to Ca2+ signaling in single cell migration in vitro as early as 20 years ago.
source: While mechanically activated ion channels were proposed to contribute to Ca2+ signaling in single cell migration in vitro as early as 20 years ago (Lee et al., 1999; Doyle et al., 2004; Wei et al., 2009; Tsai and Meyer, 2012; Patkunarajah et al., 2020), many important questions have remained unanswered, including those related to channel identity, functional effects in collective cell migration, and physiological contribution during wound healing.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 1999, Doyle et al., 2004, Wei et al., 2009, Tsai and Meyer, 2012, and Patkunarajah et al., 2020.

claim: The effects observed on scratch wound closure and cell edge retraction speeds following Yoda1 activation of PIEZO1 were consistently larger than the effects of Piezo1-GoF mutation.
source: Notably, the effects we observed on scratch wound closure and cell edge retraction speeds following Yoda1 activation of PIEZO1 were consistently larger than the effects of Piezo1-GoF mutation.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of data from Yoda1 treatment and GoF mutation experiments.

claim: The GoF mutation increases ion flux through PIEZO1 channels, without significantly affecting channel activation.
source: This is not surprising as the GoF mutation increases ion flux through PIEZO1 channels, without significantly affecting channel activation (Glogowska et al., 2017; Bae et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Glogowska et al., 2017 and Bae et al., 2013.

claim: Channel activation in GoF keratinocytes is expected to occur based on subcellular localization of PIEZO1 and of the cellular forces that activate them.
source: Thus, channel activation in GoF keratinocytes is expected to occur based on subcellular localization of PIEZO1 and of the cellular forces that activate them.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the properties of the GoF mutation.

claim: Yoda1 treatment would globally activate PIEZO1 channels in the plasma membrane, leading to a larger effect.
source: In contrast, Yoda1 treatment would globally activate PIEZO1 channels in the plasma membrane, leading to a larger effect.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the mechanism of action of Yoda1.

claim: Spatiotemporal enrichment of PIEZO1 channels serves to localize and amplify channel activity, and regulate contractile forces, to spatially control cellular retraction events.
source: Based on this finding, we propose a novel mechanism regulating cell migration wherein spatiotemporal enrichment of PIEZO1 channels serves to localize and amplify channel activity, and regulate contractile forces, to spatially control cellular retraction events.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on observations of PIEZO1 localization dynamics.

claim: Piezo1 has been implicated in cell migration in different cell types in vitro.
source: Piezo1 has been implicated in cell migration in different cell types in vitro (Maneshi et al., 2018; McHugh et al., 2012; Chubinskiy-Nadezhdin et al., 2019; Hung et al., 2016; Li et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2020); however, reports of the effect of the channel on migration have varied in the literature, with channel activity supporting migration in some cell types and inhibiting migration in others.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: A determining factor of PIEZO1's impact on cell migration may be how spatiotemporal localization of the channel is regulated in a given cell type.

evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the findings of this study.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations of PIEZO1 suggest that interactions between neighboring PIEZO1 channels may enable cooperative gating between channels.
source: Interestingly, molecular dynamics simulations of PIEZO1 suggest that interactions between neighboring PIEZO1 channels may enable cooperative gating between channels (Jiang et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jiang et al., 2021.

claim: Clustering of the bacterial mechanosensitive channel MscL has been reported.
source: Clustering of the bacterial mechanosensitive channel MscL has also been reported, but computational simulations predict these clusters in fact decrease channel open probability, providing a defence against unwanted channel gating that may cause osmotic shock (Paraschiv et al., 2020; Grage et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Paraschiv et al., 2020 and Grage et al., 2011.

claim: Computational simulations predict that MscL clusters decrease channel open probability, providing a defence against unwanted channel gating that may cause osmotic shock.

claim: Experimental evidence for functional interaction between PIEZO1 channels remains pending.
source: Experimental evidence for functional interaction between PIEZO1 channels remains pending and two recent patch clamp studies examining this question come to divergent conclusions (Lewis and Grandl, 2021; Wijerathne et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lewis and Grandl, 2021 and Wijerathne et al., 2021.

claim: Retraction during cell migration occurs due to force generated by myosin II.
source: It is well established that retraction during cell migration occurs due to force generated by myosin II (Cramer, 2013; Ridley, 2011; Aguilar-Cuenca et al., 2014), and we previously showed that myosin II-mediated cellular traction forces elicit localized Piezo1 Ca2+ flickers (Ellefsen et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cramer, 2013, Ridley, 2011, and Aguilar-Cuenca et al., 2014.

claim: Myosin II-mediated cellular traction forces elicit localized Piezo1 Ca2+ flickers.
source: It is well established that retraction during cell migration occurs due to force generated by myosin II (Cramer, 2013; Ridley, 2011; Aguilar-Cuenca et al., 2014), and we previously showed that myosin II-mediated cellular traction forces elicit localized Piezo1 Ca2+ flickers (Ellefsen et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ellefsen et al., 2019.

claim: Myosin II activation is enhanced by intracellular Ca2+.
source: Since myosin II activation is enhanced by intracellular Ca2+ (Somlyo and Somlyo, 2003), we speculate that Piezo1 may induce cellular retraction through a feedforward loop between Piezo1 and myosin II: traction force generation by myosin II cause Piezo1-mediated Ca2+ influx, which in turn may increase myosin II phosphorylation and force generation through the Ca2+-regulated Myosin Light Chain Kinase.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Somlyo and Somlyo, 2003.

claim: Piezo1 may induce cellular retraction through a feedforward loop between Piezo1 and myosin II.
source: Since myosin II activation is enhanced by intracellular Ca2+ (Somlyo and Somlyo, 2003), we speculate that Piezo1 may induce cellular retraction through a feedforward loop between Piezo1 and myosin II: traction force generation by myosin II cause Piezo1-mediated Ca2+ influx, which in turn may increase myosin II phosphorylation and force generation through the Ca2+-regulated Myosin Light Chain Kinase.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on known properties of myosin II and Piezo1.

claim: Enrichment of Piezo1 in subcellular regions would amplify the feedforward loop effect and result in a localized retraction.
source: Enrichment of Piezo1 in subcellular regions would amplify this effect and result in a localized retraction.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the proposed feedforward loop mechanism.

claim: Piezo1-mediated Ca2+ events elicit retraction of developing endothelial tip cells during vascular pathfinding.
source: Supporting this model, Piezo1-mediated Ca2+ events were recently found to elicit retraction of developing endothelial tip cells during vascular pathfinding (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2020.

claim: Efficient migration requires protrusion of the cell lamellipodia which is stabilized via the formation of focal adhesions.
source: Efficient migration requires protrusion of the cell lamellipodia which is stabilized via the formation of focal adhesions.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about cell migration.

claim: Without stabilization, lamellipodia protrusions retract backward causing membrane ruffling and reducing migration speed.
source: Without stabilization, lamellipodia protrusions retract backward causing membrane ruffling and reducing migration speed (Borm et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Borm et al., 2005.

claim: PIEZO1-mediated effects on cell edge velocity may be the predominant mechanism contributing to inefficient migration.
source: We observe an increase in cell edge velocity in keratinocytes with increased PIEZO1 activity (in both Piezo1-GoF and Yoda1-treated cells) indicating that PIEZO1-mediated effects on cell edge velocity may be the predominant mechanism contributing to inefficient migration.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of increased cell edge velocity in GoF and Yoda1-treated cells.

claim: Both Piezo1-cKO and Piezo1-GoF keratinocytes exhibit straighter migration trajectories.
source: An intriguing paradox observed in our data is that both Piezo1-cKO and Piezo1-GoF keratinocytes exhibit straighter migration trajectories.
evidence: The claim is supported by direction autocorrelation analyses in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3D.

claim: PIEZO1 localization and increased activity appears linked to cell polarization.
source: We also observe that PIEZO1 localization and increased activity appears linked to cell polarization; thus one possible explanation that warrants further study is that the GoF mutation stabilizes PIEZO1 clusters so that once the channels localize to the rear of the cell, the cell retains its polarization and migration directionality.
evidence: The claim is supported by VAMPIRE shape mode analyses in Figure 3.

claim: The GoF mutation may stabilize PIEZO1 clusters so that once the channels localize to the rear of the cell, the cell retains its polarization and migration directionality.

evidence: The claim is speculative, proposed as a possible explanation for the observed paradox.

claim: Cell migration involves a complex orchestration of events, including sub-cellular dynamics in which cytoskeletal processes in different compartments of the cell need to be implemented in a precise spatiotemporal order.
source: Cell migration involves a complex orchestration of events, including sub-cellular dynamics in which cytoskeletal processes in different compartments of the cell need to be implemented in a precise spatiotemporal order.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about cell migration.

claim: Spatiotemporal enrichment dynamics of Piezo1 play a role in coordinating cytoskeletal processes during cell migration.
source: Our findings suggest that spatiotemporal enrichment dynamics of Piezo1 play a role in this coordination.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the findings of this study.

claim: Nanoscale spatial dynamics of Piezo1 channels can control tissue-scale events.
source: More broadly, our findings provide a mechanism by which nanoscale spatial dynamics of Piezo1 channels can control tissue-scale events, a finding with implications beyond wound healing to processes as diverse as development, homeostasis, disease, and repair.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the findings of this study and speculates on broader implications.

claim: The findings have implications beyond wound healing to processes as diverse as development, homeostasis, disease, and repair.

claim: The skin is the largest organ of the body.
source: The skin, the largest organ of the body, serves as a barrier against a myriad of external insults while also performing important sensory and homeostatic functions.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge.

claim: The skin serves as a barrier against external insults while also performing important sensory and homeostatic functions.
source: The skin, the largest organ of the body, serves as a barrier against a myriad of external insults while also performing important sensory and homeostatic functions.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge.

claim: Cutaneous wounds interfere with skin functions and expose the body to an increased risk of infection, disease, and scar formation.
source: Cutaneous wounds interfere with all these functions and expose the body to an increased risk of infection, disease, and scar formation (Evans et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Evans et al., 2013.

claim: The migration of keratinocytes from the wound edge into the wound bed plays an essential step in re-establishing the epithelial barrier during repair of wounded skin.
source: During the repair of wounded skin, the migration of keratinocytes from the wound edge into the wound bed plays an essential step in re-establishing the epithelial barrier and restoring its protective functions (Kirfel and Herzog, 2004; Gantwerker and Hom, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kirfel and Herzog, 2004 and Gantwerker and Hom, 2011.

claim: Mechanical cues and cell-generated traction forces in keratinocytes play an important role in regulating the healing process and wound closure.
source: Accumulating evidence has shown that mechanical cues and cell-generated traction forces in keratinocytes play an important role in regulating the healing process and wound closure (Evans et al., 2013; Rosińczuk et al., 2016; Brugués, 2014; Hiroyasu et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2017; Ladoux and Mège, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The molecular identity of keratinocyte mechanotransducers that control re-epithelialization remains unknown.
source: However, the molecular identity of keratinocyte mechanotransducers that control re-epithelialization remains unknown.
evidence: The claim is based on the state of knowledge at the time of the study.

claim: Mechanically activated ion channels offer the unique ability for cells to rapidly detect and transduce mechanical forces into electrochemical signals.
source: One class of mechanosensors utilized by cells are mechanically activated ion channels which offer the unique ability for cells to rapidly detect and transduce mechanical forces into electrochemical signals (Nourse and Pathak, 2017; Murthy et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nourse and Pathak, 2017 and Murthy et al., 2017.

claim: The Piezo1 ion channel plays an important role in a variety of cell types and regulates several key biological processes.
source: The Piezo1 ion channel has been shown to play an important role in a variety of cell types, and it regulates several key biological processes including vascular and lymphatic development, red blood cell volume regulation, stem cell fate, the baroreceptor response, cardiovascular homeostasis, cartilage mechanics, and others (Li et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014; Pathak et al., 2014; Rocio Servin-Vences et al., 2017; Zeng et al., 2018; Nonomura et al., 2018; Cahalan et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2014; Rode et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Previous studies in MDCK cells and in zebrafish larvae have demonstrated the importance of Piezo1 in homeostatic regulation of epithelial cell numbers.
source: Previous studies in MDCK cells and in zebrafish larvae have demonstrated the importance of the channel in homeostatic regulation of epithelial cell numbers (Gudipaty et al., 2017; Eisenhoffer et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gudipaty et al., 2017 and Eisenhoffer et al., 2012.

claim: PIEZO1 activity increases cellular retraction, reducing the efficiency of keratinocyte migration and wound healing.
source: Here, we show that PIEZO1 activity increases cellular retraction, reducing the efficiency of keratinocyte migration and wound healing, and that inhibition of PIEZO1 results in faster wound healing in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experiments shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: Inhibition of PIEZO1 results in faster wound healing in vitro and in vivo.

evidence: The claim is supported by wound healing assays in Piezo1-cKO mice and cells.
